regions.full_page: And you hestitate not to commend as a sane view, in regard to Ireland, the dictum of one holding his title of honor and his commission from that same intriguing, hypocirtical power? And look how you quote him! Nearly half a column! Let me cite just a line or two from your quotation, " ... Therefore, my first word to you about Ireland is: Do not be too much dis- turbed by rumors about affairs in Ireland. "Ireland is on the way to Peace." Smoothe words indeed! How soothing to anxious souls in America! Do you not suspect the polished parallel of the referred to Agencies and Newspapers. Is the meaning of these words of Lord Shaw satisfactorily clear to you? They are not so to me. I would ask: Does your hero - if he be not a wily Briton - get his inspiration from the President of Ireland or from the Primer of England? Is it Cromwelian Peace he predicts, or is it the Peace for which Pearse and Comrades died in 1916 and since, down to MacSwiney and Brugha and Boland? Is it finally the peace for which DeValera and comrades are still holding out, which God only can give -- and is giving shortly - or what Shaw's King would be satisfied to call Peace? Do not forget that he tells you plainly that he is, "talking as an old Politician" - a British one, of course. Strange he did not know that his title assures us that he was both, before he was lorded. Ah Shaw! "Do not be too much disturbed -- "lest it be once more officially probed and found that your government's welfare work in Ireland still "stinks" in the nostrils of civilization "worse than it did eighteen months ago. Now before quoting from an acknowledged adept at lingual smoothness and duplicity - "an old politician", before poor Shaw was born or thought of, and undoubtedly as active in 20th century politics as any of his titled juniors - let me assure you that your correspondent is not doing this in any spirit of vindictiveness or out of malice to any one. He wishes simply to save, not only The Catholic News, but as much as he can, the honest press in general from humiliation more serious than any honest criticism could be, and that must come unless something be dore to arrest the above lamented in- clination of positively favoring British views, and British Calumnies, and worst of all because more dangerous, British Colored Truths. Who will doubt, at second thought and in the light of the present British-Begotten and British-fostered - and I must say British-waged War in Ireland that the above words of Lord Shaw are at least a weak parallel to those we find in the Third Chapter of Holy Writ? Here they follow: "And the Serpent said to the Woman: No, you shall not die the death, for God doth know that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil." (Gen . 111, 4) That is just an example of colored truth and of dubious prediction. No one doubts that their eyes were opened. But alas for their vision! and alas for your vision and mine! Alas, too, for peace and Ireland unless the Lord deliver her from Shaw and his kind, and from the peace they would wish for the Ireland of the Saints! God help our civilization at all events, for its hopelessly darkened understanding. We sometimes wonder at the simplicity of our poor first Parents and at their docile blindness toward their seducer. Yet, with all our science and with all the manifestation of historic ages, we refuse to recognize -- nay even to suspect-behind the blasphemous press of to-day, the same power that animated the wretched serpent. Aye,
